Essentials 2.0 · Flow inspiration · 07-reports

Reports: ideas from other products

This page shows examples from other products for center-wide and cross-course reporting in Essentials 2.0, grouped by product. It covers scheduled summary reports for deans, comparing groups of learners, reviewing and approving AI evaluations, headline numbers (KPIs) on how rooms, equipment and people are used, and easy sharing. Reports from inside a single course are covered in courses/08-recordings-course-reports. This page is about sending reports out and about center-level numbers. Sources: the design reference libraries Mobbin and Refero (web products), researched on 30 September 2026.

What we have today. Today Essentials has four reports: Responses, Group Performance, Performance Matrix and Skill Development. Skill areas depend on naming abbreviations used across the program. An activity must be assigned before data is collected, so late setup loses data. Accreditation packs are put together by hand. Utilisation reporting is the one report every center we visited wants and none can get. The plan has five parts. Deans get an automatic weekly or monthly PDF or newsletter, shared by link. Learner feedback and faculty grading sit in one place and can be compared by course, year, learner or period. Headline numbers show sim and room usage and faculty hours, taken from the calendar. Formative work gets a colour or narrative scale, and AI writes formative and summative reports. Deep report builders are left out of the first version, in favour of ready-made defaults that need no setup.

How to read this page

Each section below is one product. Each strip of screenshots is one flow: a real sequence of screens, in the order a user sees them. Click a screenshot to enlarge it. "Worth borrowing" lists ideas we could use, and "Avoid" lists what we should not copy. Use the task filters to see only one task, and click ☆ on a flow to add it to your own shortlist.

12 products · 21 flows · 103 screens · 5 tasks

What the best products have in common

  1. Subscribe to the view you are looking at Amplitude and Mixpanel attach a schedule and a channel (email or Slack) to the live dashboard, instead of using a separate report builder. Later adds a one-switch Monday digest and a public link that keeps itself up to date. By default, Essentials should send weekly or monthly packs to deans from the center dashboard, with a pause option, rather than offer a chart editor.See: Amplitude: Subscribing to dashboard reports · Mixpanel: Subscribing a board (email) · Later: Enabling an email report · Later: Creating a performance report
  2. Compare by regrouping, not by building charts Mixpanel lets you switch between 'Time Period', 'Segment' and '% Overall'. 15Five shows self, manager and peer ratings on one competency scale and regroups the same numbers by manager. Both show how groups and raters line up without anyone designing a chart. In Essentials, this means filters by course, year, learner and faculty on Group Performance and Performance Matrix.See: Mixpanel: Selecting segments · Mixpanel: Comparing insight (time periods) · 15Five: Competency assessment · 15Five: Breakdown
  3. AI drafts are never sent automatically Charma limits the tags the AI can use, shows several suggestions, requires an edit before 'Submit', and shows 'hasn't seen this yet' until the person reads it. Fireflies uses section checklists and shows clearly when a section is empty. Dialpad changes the recap length next to the transcript it is based on, then shares a link. For Essentials, formative feedback means narrative sections, and summative grading stays scored elsewhere.See: Charma: Generating feedback suggestions · Charma: Giving a peer review · Charma: Editing and sending feedback · Fireflies: Customizing a summary · Dialpad: Updating a recap with AI
  4. Usage in a clearly defined unit, with the change since last period Whereby's 'Participant Minutes' (with a hint explaining the unit) and Cal.com's booking numbers with 'from last period' arrows make usage easy to read. Cal.com's people-by-week grid and Deputy's hours catalog could extend to faculty contact hours. Room and sim minutes taken from the calendar are more useful than engagement charts that only look impressive.See: Whereby: Insights · Whereby: Room detail · Cal.com: View bookings insight · Cal.com: View routing insight · Deputy: Analytics
  5. Sharing with deans: a link with an expiry date, or a PDF by email Juicebox splits Export into a password-protected web link, a download, or a PDF or image by email. Midday shares a snapshot of one number with an explicit expiry date. Later's public report link, with its view count, is what a newsletter would point to. Leadership should not need an Essentials login.See: Juicebox: Sharing dashboard to web · Juicebox: Sending to email · Midday: Sharing a metric · Later: Creating a performance report
  6. Avoid built-in report builders Deputy's catalog promotes scheduled summaries and PDFs, but it also leads into a Sigma-style report builder. Treat that as the example of what not to do. The first version of Essentials should ship ready-made templates (usage, group performance, AI formative feedback) rather than a blank page.See: Deputy: Analytics

Questions we still need to answer

  • Robin and Envoy, which measure real workplace usage, never appeared in Mobbin's web results. Cal.com, Whereby and Deputy are the nearest examples from other fields. How far can bookings and participant minutes stand in for camera hours in sim rooms?
  • We found few examples of what the recipient sees in an email or PDF newsletter; most screens showed writing or subscribing. What does a dean's inbox view need beyond a link and a PDF attachment?
  • Going from a course overview down to one learner is already covered in courses/08. How should center-wide comparison hand over to a course report without repeating the Kajabi and SchoolAI patterns?
  • Fireflies' sections and Charma's competency tags hint at a colour or narrative scale for formative work. But no product showed a traffic-light formative score in place of points, so that is still to be designed.
  • Dashboards across several campuses raise hard questions about who can see what. None of the shortlisted flows solve access control across separate organizations.
  • Most Refero examples had only one screenshot and were dropped. Is another Refero search worth it to fill the gap on what digest recipients see?

Mixpanel

Same task, different field3 flows

Mixpanel lets you subscribe to the live board you are looking at, by email or Slack, on a schedule. It also has a grid that splits results by group and a 'Compare' option for periods or groups, without a report builder.

WebMobbin5 steps

Subscribing a board (email)

From a board's 'Subscribe' pop-up, the user creates a weekly subscription with a day, time, time zone and a recipient found by search.

Automatic weekly or monthly reports

Worth borrowing

  • 'Subscribe' sits on the board next to 'Share', so you subscribe to the view you are looking at (screen 1).
  • Email and Slack are tabs in the same window, so choosing a channel needs no separate steps (screens 2 to 5).
  • 'Send Test' sits next to the subscriber list, so you can check the digest before it goes live (screens 2 to 5).
  • When there are no subscriptions, the screen says 'No email subscriptions found for this board' and offers 'Create New' (screen 1).

Avoid

  • Day, time and time zone must all be set before anything is sent, with no default, which works against ready-made weekly digests for deans (screens 2 to 3).

What it means for Essentials Reports: subscribing from the board becomes an automatic weekly or monthly email for deans. It adds to today's reports, which are pulled by hand, without a report builder.

View on Mobbin ↗
WebMobbin4 steps

Selecting segments

The user builds an analysis with two measures, split by device type and user group, then chooses which groups show in the chart and table.

Compare performance by learner, group, semester, course, or faculty

Worth borrowing

  • Rows nest by measure, then device type, then group, with an average and a column per day, so groups can be compared in one grid (screens 1 to 4).
  • Coloured checkboxes in the table also control the chart lines, so one control updates both views (screens 2 to 4).
  • Labels in the query panel name each split, such as device type or group, instead of hiding them in filters (screens 1 to 4).

Avoid

  • A full query builder (measures, filters, splits) as the first version goes against the plan to ship ready-made defaults rather than deep builders (screens 1 to 4).

What it means for Essentials Reports: this maps to comparing groups by course, year and learner in Performance Matrix and Group Performance. Essentials should ship it as ready-made views, not a free-form analysis tool.

View on Mobbin ↗
WebMobbin6 steps

Comparing insight (time periods)

From a chart, the user turns on a comparison with the previous period and sees 'Past Avg' columns with the change shown as green or red percentages.

Compare performance by learner, group, semester, course, or faculty

Worth borrowing

  • The 'Compare' menu separates 'Time Period', 'Segment' and '% Overall', so comparing periods and comparing groups are not mixed in one control (screens 3 to 4).
  • Presets for the previous day, 7 days, 30 days, 3 months and a year, plus a custom option, cover most comparisons without picking dates (screen 4).
  • A 'Compare to previous day' label, 'Past Avg' columns and percentage changes show what moved at a glance (screens 5 to 6).

What it means for Essentials Reports: compare this period with the last for room use and for faculty or learner headline numbers. It extends Performance Matrix, but does not help with accreditation packs.

Amplitude

Same task, different field1 flow

Amplitude sets up a dashboard subscription with one plain sentence, 'Every [day] at [time]'. It is the clearest scheduled report that works without any setup.

WebMobbin3 steps

Subscribing to dashboard reports

From a dashboard's 'Subscribe' button, the user sets up a recurring email or Slack delivery with a one-line schedule, a CSV file and subscribers, then edits the saved subscription.

Automatic weekly or monthly reports

Worth borrowing

  • The schedule reads as one sentence, 'Every [day] at [time]', with a CSV attachment (screen 2).
  • A time zone line ('Showing times as...') sits above the schedule, so recipients on different campuses share one clock (screens 2 to 3).
  • After saving, a green message appears and the schedule stays editable, so you can pause or change it without starting over (screen 3).
  • A search box under the schedule adds subscribers, which supports digests for people who may not have an account (screens 2 to 3).

Avoid

  • CSV is the only default format, but deans need a PDF or a written newsletter rather than a raw data file (screens 2 to 3).

What it means for Essentials Reports: the closest pattern for automatic weekly or monthly digests for deans from a fixed dashboard. It is a ready-made subscription instead of packs put together by hand.

Later

Same task, different field2 flows

Later has an on/off switch to pause its Monday email, and a public report link that updates itself and shows how often it was viewed. That covers pausing a digest and sharing with a dean who has no account.

WebMobbin3 steps

Enabling an email report

In Account Settings, the user reads the fixed Monday schedule for the analytics email, switches it on for one profile, and sees a confirmation.

Automatic weekly or monthly reports

Worth borrowing

  • The schedule is fixed ('Emails are sent each Monday in the late afternoon (Pacific Time)'), so the only choice is on or off (screens 1 to 2).
  • A switch per profile, plus 'Enable All' and 'Disable All', pauses the email without losing the settings (screens 1 to 2).
  • The confirmation names the profile and repeats when the email goes out (screen 3).

Avoid

  • The digest is buried in Account Settings, far from Analytics; for deans, the subscribe option belongs on the report itself (screen 1).

What it means for Essentials Reports: the simplest weekly or monthly newsletter for deans, with one default schedule and a pause switch instead of a report builder.

View on Mobbin ↗
WebMobbin5 steps

Creating a performance report

From the analytics overview, the user creates a shareable performance report, waits for its unique link, sets it to update automatically, and copies the public link.

Easy sharing of reportsAutomatic weekly or monthly reports

Worth borrowing

  • A public report link with 'Copy Link' and a view count lets people see the report without an Essentials account (screens 4 to 5).
  • 'Update Report Automatically' every 24 hours keeps the link current instead of a one-off export (screen 4).
  • An 'Enable Report' switch turns the report off without losing its settings (screen 4).
  • Sharing starts from the overview, next to the headline numbers, not from the settings (screen 1).

What it means for Essentials Reports: a report pack for deans or accreditation, shared by link without accounts. Automatic refresh comes close to a scheduled digest, and the industry comparison hints at benchmarks without a builder.

15Five

Close match2 flows

15Five shows self, manager and peer ratings on the same competency scale and can regroup the numbers by manager. It is the closest match to comparing faculty and learner scoring.

WebMobbin5 steps

Competency assessment

In a quarterly review, the user compares self, manager and peer ratings on one competency scale, then opens each competency to see the written answer behind it.

Compare performance by learner, group, semester, course, or faculty

Worth borrowing

  • Coloured checkboxes for Self, Manager and Peer show or hide their ratings on one competency scale, so comparing raters needs no second report (screens 3 to 4).
  • 'Top competencies' and 'Top opportunities' boxes above the grid show strengths and areas to grow before the full list (screen 3).
  • A highlighted note explains that the graph shows how far raters agree, which teaches the reader how to use it (screen 2).
  • Each competency links to its written answer ('1 answer'), so you can go from a score to the reasoning (screen 5).

Avoid

  • The full grid still shows when manager or peer ratings are missing; in sim, raters without ratings should stay hidden until there is data (screens 3 to 4).

What it means for Essentials Reports: adds comparison from several points of view, with a path to the evidence, to Performance Matrix and Skill Development. It suits learner and faculty dashboards rather than a PDF newsletter for deans.

View on Mobbin ↗
WebMobbin3 steps

Breakdown

On the outcomes dashboard, the user moves past empty summary boxes to 'Breakdown' and compares results by manager, with company-wide and 'No manager' rows.

Compare performance by learner, group, semester, course, or faculty

Worth borrowing

  • A 'Compare by' list regroups the same columns by manager, so switching between learner, faculty or course would need no builder (screens 2 to 3).
  • A company-wide row above the team rows lets you compare one unit with the whole organization (screens 2 to 3).
  • 'Who else can see this?' and 'Configure' sit next to the table, so visibility is set where the comparison is (screen 2).

Avoid

  • Empty summary screens show sales buttons ('Schedule survey', 'Configure performance'); Essentials should say plainly that data is missing (screen 1).

What it means for Essentials Reports: a pattern for comparable tables of faculty or course numbers (room, simulator and faculty hours) that can be regrouped. The empty summary screens do not fit reporting that starts with room use.

Charma

Close match3 flows

Charma's FeedbackAI drafts feedback from a fixed set of tags. A person picks and edits a draft before sending, and can see when it has not been read yet. This is the review loop for AI evaluations.

WebMobbin6 steps

Generating feedback suggestions

The user picks strength and improvement tags, waits up to about 30 seconds for FeedbackAI, then chooses one of three AI drafts to edit.

AI evaluation (formative and summative)

Worth borrowing

  • Tag fields, with a limit of two areas to improve, narrow what the AI writes about before it starts (screens 1 to 2).
  • The loading text says it can take up to 30 seconds and shows placeholder bars, so the wait is expected (screen 3).
  • The user chooses from three suggestions or asks for new ones, so a person picks the tone before editing (screens 4 to 6).
  • A note under the card says the text comes from GPT-3, so readers know the formative feedback is AI-written (screens 3 to 6).

Avoid

  • The AI drafts repeat playful custom tags ('good potato') in the feedback; clinical wording has to be checked and tied to competencies (screens 5 to 6).

What it means for Essentials Reports: an AI-drafted formative note for faculty, written from competency tags. It adds to Responses and Skill Development, not to accreditation packs.

View on Mobbin ↗
WebMobbin10 steps

Giving a peer review

From the open 360 reviews, the user writes an anonymous peer review from chosen adjectives, lets FeedbackAI draft the text, reviews and submits it, and sees '1 of 2' progress.

AI evaluation (formative and summative)

Worth borrowing

  • A 'How it works' screen explains that chosen adjectives feed FeedbackAI and that peers stay anonymous, so privacy and the AI's role are clear before starting (screen 2).
  • 'Generate Feedback' drafts text from the chosen adjectives, and the user is asked to 'sprinkle in specific examples' (screens 3 to 5).
  • A review screen gathers the tags and text for every competency before 'Submit' (screens 7 to 8).
  • After sending, the person who asked for reviews sees a '1 of 2 reviews submitted' progress bar (screens 1 and 10).

Avoid

  • An emoji and GIF toolbar in the feedback editor is too casual for summative clinical reports (screens 5 to 6).

What it means for Essentials Reports: an AI write-up of formative feedback from peers or faculty, based on competency labels. Pooling answers anonymously fits reports with several raters per skill, not room-use numbers.

View on Mobbin ↗
WebMobbin4 steps

Editing and sending feedback

The user picks an AI suggestion, edits it and submits, then sees the feedback marked 'Jon hasn't seen this yet', with Edit and Delete still available.

AI evaluation (formative and summative)

Worth borrowing

  • The chosen draft opens for editing before 'Submit', so AI text is never sent automatically (screens 1 to 2).
  • A 'hasn't seen this yet' status on the shared feedback shows whether it has been read (screens 3 to 4).
  • Edit and Delete stay available until it is read, so faculty can take feedback back before the learner opens it (screens 3 to 4).

What it means for Essentials Reports: a faculty note written after the AI draft, with control over when it is seen. Useful for formative learner reports before PDFs are shared with deans.

Fireflies

Same task, different field1 flow

Fireflies lets you tick which sections a summary should have (Outline, Blockers and more), applies them with 'Save & Apply', and shows clearly when Blockers is empty. That suits formative narrative feedback better than a free-text prompt.

WebMobbin5 steps

Customizing a summary

On a meeting page, the user picks which sections the AI summary should include, taps 'Save & Apply', waits while it regenerates, then reads the notes, including an empty Blockers section.

AI evaluation (formative and summative)

Worth borrowing

  • A checklist of sections, each saying in plain words what the AI will pull out, shapes the report without a builder (screens 2 to 3).
  • 'Save' keeps the preferences, and 'Save & Apply' also regenerates this meeting's summary straight away (screen 3).
  • A processing message while the transcript is analysed again is honest about the AI wait (screen 4).
  • An empty section says 'No blockers were explicitly discussed' instead of disappearing, so the absence is clear (screen 5).

Avoid

  • Sales and meeting templates (BANT, Standup) in the same list are the wrong lens for clinical simulation; keep only debrief and competency templates (screen 1).

What it means for Essentials Reports: an AI formative or summative report of a recorded session, with templates and section switches for debrief PDFs. It pairs with the transcript time stamps in the session video review screen (SRV), not with Performance Matrix.

Dialpad

Same task, different field1 flow

Dialpad changes the length of its call recap right next to the transcript and @comments, then shares it by link. This is editing and approving with the evidence in view.

WebMobbin5 steps

Updating a recap with AI

On a call review, the user reads the AI recap, picks a summary length, waits while it regenerates, and gets a longer recap that can still be shared.

AI evaluation (formative and summative)Easy sharing of reports

Worth borrowing

  • A length menu (Short, Medium, Long, Bulleted) regenerates the recap in place with one control (screens 3 to 5).
  • A wait message on the recap while it reformats shows that the change is in progress (screen 4).
  • Time-stamped comments with @mentions next to the recap let faculty add notes to the same session report (screens 1 to 2).
  • 'Copy link' and 'Share' in the call review header make sharing by link the default (screens 1 and 5).

Avoid

  • An empty Moments column with nothing to do should be hidden or explained until there are highlights (screens 1 to 5).

What it means for Essentials Reports: an AI session recap with a length control and link sharing. It fits formative summaries for faculty or deans, not tables of room-use numbers.

Cal.com

Same task, different field2 flows

Cal.com shows booking headline numbers with the change since the last period, plus a grid of people by week. It is a model for room and time-slot usage.

WebMobbin6 steps

View bookings insight

The user opens booking insights, picks an account or team and the last 7 days, scans the headline boxes and trend chart, then the rankings of team members.

Totals for simulation and resource use (headline numbers)

Worth borrowing

  • Each headline box shows a value, a coloured arrow and 'from last period', so performance can be compared without a builder (screens 1 to 4).
  • The trend chart shows Created, Completed, Rescheduled and Cancelled as separate lines, with a hint for each day (screen 4).
  • Rankings for Most Booked, Least Booked and Most Cancelled team members show use per person, as you would want for faculty (screens 5 to 6).
  • When there are no ratings yet, a 'Workflows' button offers to start collecting them (screen 6).

Avoid

  • Eight boxes that are always shown, many with zeros and 0% change, are noisy for small sim centers; fewer numbers, led by room use, work better (screens 1 to 3).

What it means for Essentials Reports: fills the gap for room use, with room and faculty-hour numbers from the calendar and comparable performance. Its download is a light export, not a digest sent to deans by link.

View on Mobbin ↗
WebMobbin4 steps

View routing insight

The user filters routing insights by team and form and reads the funnel boxes and response table. They then view bookings per person by day, week or month, and failed bookings by form answer.

Totals for simulation and resource use (headline numbers)

Worth borrowing

  • Three headline boxes follow the funnel: 'Total Responses', 'Without Booking' and 'With Booking' (screens 1 to 2).
  • A day, week or month switch and a grid of people by period show each person's load, like faculty hours (screen 3).
  • Horizontal bars break down failed bookings by the answers given in the form (screen 4).
  • Segment, Save, Clear and Download sit on the report itself (screens 1 to 2).

What it means for Essentials Reports: a strong model for use per person by week or month. It matches the time periods of automatic digests for deans without a deep report builder.

Whereby

Same task, different field2 flows

Whereby lists participant minutes and opens one room's detail, with the unit clearly defined. It is a model for boxes showing simulator and room contact hours.

WebMobbin2 steps

Insights

The user lands on a 'Get started' page showing the plan's remaining minutes. They then open the rooms list to see when each room was last active, its participant minutes and its session count.

Totals for simulation and resource use (headline numbers)

Worth borrowing

  • A plan label on the side always shows the participant minutes left, like a usage budget (screens 1 to 2).
  • The rooms list shows 'Last active', 'PM used' and 'Sessions' for each room (screen 2).
  • A small hint on the column header explains Participant Minutes (PM) while you read the number (screen 2).

Avoid

  • The flow opens on a welcome page before the insights; room use should not sit behind a getting-started screen (screen 1).

What it means for Essentials Reports: a direct match for sim-room use, from the room list to minutes and sessions. It moves Essentials toward room-hour numbers taken from the calendar.

Room detail

The user opens the rooms list, shows the hint that defines Participant Minutes (PM), then opens one room's details with summary boxes and a log of PM per session.

Deputy

Same task, different field1 flow

Deputy has a catalog of workforce reports and promotes scheduled summary emails. Its path into a Sigma-style report builder, where you build charts from scratch, is something to avoid.

WebMobbin10 steps

Analytics

The user opens Analytics, sets up a schedule-adherence report for one team member with a tolerance, loads the comparison table, then browses the audit, attendance, map and turnover reports.

Totals for simulation and resource use (headline numbers)Compare performance by learner, group, semester, course, or facultyAutomatic weekly or monthly reports

Worth borrowing

  • The welcome text offers three ways out: download a spreadsheet, print a PDF, or schedule the report to the people who need it (screen 3).
  • A tolerance (15 minutes) is chosen before the adherence data loads (screens 4 to 6).
  • Planned shifts and actual timesheets sit side by side, with differences in hours and cost shown in red (screen 6).
  • The Analytics home shows 'Shift Pulse' as a 4/5 average with a small trend line and a recent comment: a formative score with a narrative (screen 2).

Avoid

  • The catalog of business-intelligence reports, with '+ Create report' and 'Make a copy', is built on Sigma. It goes against the plan of no deep report builders in the first version (screens 3 to 10).

What it means for Essentials Reports: borrow the scheduled delivery, the comparisons of planned and actual use, and the formative pulse. Do not bring over the embedded report library.

Juicebox

Same task, different field2 flows

Juicebox puts three options in one Export menu: share to the web with a password, download, or email a PDF or image. That covers sending a report to a dean who has no account.

WebMobbin5 steps

Sharing dashboard to web

From an analytics page, the user opens 'Export', chooses 'Share to web', sets a password and whether viewers may use filters, then gets a link to copy.

Easy sharing of reports

Worth borrowing

  • One 'Export' menu offers 'Share to web', 'Download' and 'Send to email' (screen 2).
  • The shared page needs a password, set before or together with the link (screens 3 to 5).
  • A switch, 'Allow viewers to interact with filters', decides whether viewers can use the page's filters (screens 3 to 5).
  • Once set up, the live link is ready to paste (screen 5).

Avoid

  • The link lives on another company's site (explo.co); links for deans should sit under the Essentials domain (screen 5).

What it means for Essentials Reports: the closest pattern to automatic digests shared by link: a report link with an optional password and control over what viewers can change.

Sending to email

The user opens 'Export', chooses 'Send to email', picks PDF or image, enters a recipient, and sees 'Email will be sent shortly'.

Easy sharing of reports

  • The user picks PDF or image before sending (screens 2 to 4).

Midday

Same task, different field1 flow

Midday shares a snapshot of a single number through a public link with a set expiry date. That makes it safe to share for accreditation.

WebMobbin5 steps

Sharing a metric

The user shares one headline number (Revenue) from its box, creates a public snapshot link that expires, then opens or copies the link.

Easy sharing of reports

Worth borrowing

  • Each number has its own 'Share' option in the box's menu, instead of one export for the whole app (screen 2).
  • Before creating the link, the window explains that the chart is 'a snapshot in time' and asks for an expiry date (screen 4).
  • Once created, the link can be opened or copied, and its expiry date stays visible (screen 5).
  • The shared box has a legend for current, previous and average values (screens 1 to 2).

Avoid

  • Buttons to post on X or LinkedIn in the share window have no place in digests for deans and faculty (screen 5).

What it means for Essentials Reports: the best model for public digest links for deans that expire: one snapshot link per headline number. It is lighter than a live shared dashboard with filters.
